## Overview

This vignette introduces the workflow of `ReproductiveNumbers.jl` on the simplest
compartmental model, the SIR model. The construction follows Diekmann, Heesterbeek and
Roberts (2010), *The construction of next-generation matrices for compartmental epidemic
models* (J. R. Soc. Interface 7:873–885).

The idea is to look only at the *infected subsystem* (the compartments that can transmit
or will transmit after progression), linearise it at the infection-free steady state, and
split the resulting Jacobian into two parts:

  - the **transmission matrix** `T`, whose entry `T[i, j]` is the rate at which an
    individual in infected state `j` produces *new* infections in state `i`, and
  - the **transition matrix** `Σ`, containing every other change of state (progression,
    recovery, death), so that `-Σ⁻¹[i, j]` is the expected time an individual currently in
    state `j` will spend in state `i`.

The next-generation matrix with large domain is `K_L = -T Σ⁻¹`, and `R₀` is its spectral
radius: the expected number of new infections produced by a typical infected individual over
its whole infectious life.

## The model

```{julia}
using ReproductiveNumbers, ModelingToolkit, Symbolics
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D

@parameters β γ N
@variables S(t) I(t) R(t)
eqs = [D(S) ~ -β * S * I / N,
    D(I) ~ β * S * I / N - γ * I,
    D(R) ~ γ * I]
sir = complete(System(eqs, t; name = :sir))
```

## Building the next-generation matrix

The only infected compartment is `I`. Without births or deaths every state with `I = 0` is
a steady state, so the infection-free steady state is not unique and we have to say which
one we mean: the fully susceptible population `S = N`.

```{julia}
ngm = next_generation_matrix(sir, [I]; equilibrium = Dict(S => N, R => 0))
```

The package classified the term `β S I / N` as a transmission (it involves the uninfected
state `S`) and `-γ I` as a transition. The resulting matrices are `1 × 1`:

```{julia}
T, Σ = transmission_transition_matrices(ngm)
T, Σ
```

`-Σ⁻¹ = 1/γ` is the mean infectious period and `T = β` the transmission rate at the
infection-free steady state, so

```{julia}
basic_reproduction_number(ngm)
```

Every infected compartment here is a state-at-infection (an individual can be in it
immediately after being infected):

```{julia}
states_at_infection(ngm)
```

## Numeric evaluation

Given parameter values the same object gives a number:

```{julia}
p = Dict(β => 0.5, γ => 0.25, N => 1000.0)
basic_reproduction_number(ngm, p)
```

or, equivalently, evaluate the whole decomposition and inspect the numeric matrices:

```{julia}
evaluate(ngm, p)
```

Parameter values can also be read from an `ODEProblem` built from the same system:

```{julia}
using OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5
prob = ODEProblem(sir, [S => 999.0, I => 1.0, R => 0.0, β => 0.5, γ => 0.25, N => 1000.0],
    (0.0, 60.0))
basic_reproduction_number(ngm, prob)
```

## The threshold property

`R₀ > 1` exactly when the infection-free steady state is unstable, so an epidemic can
take off. We can confirm this by simulation:

```{julia}
using Plots
plt = plot(xlabel = "time", ylabel = "I(t)", legend = :topright)
for βval in (0.2, 0.25, 0.5)
    prob_β = remake(prob; p = [β => βval])
    sol = solve(prob_β, Tsit5())
    plot!(plt, sol; idxs = I, label = "R₀ = $(basic_reproduction_number(ngm, prob_β))")
end
plt
```

## A reproduction number at any state

The `equilibrium` keyword accepts any state. Leaving `S` symbolic gives the reproduction
number when a fraction `S/N` of the population is susceptible, i.e. the effective
reproduction number `R = R₀ S / N`:

```{julia}
ngm_S = next_generation_matrix(sir, [I]; equilibrium = Dict(R => 0))
basic_reproduction_number(ngm_S)
```
